title: One phishing email hijacked 2 billion weekly downloads

beats.say: One fake email just hijacked code that's downloaded two billion times a week.
In September twenty twenty five, a maintainer entered his password and two factor code on a page that looked like npm.
Within hours, twenty popular packages had malicious versions.
That included chalk and debug. Any app that built with those versions could ship the attacker's code to its users.
The code swapped crypto wallet addresses in the browser. The attacker made about six hundred dollars.
A week later, a self copying worm did something worse. It stole tokens and cloud keys, then published itself into over five hundred packages.

vis.title: worm: Shai-Hulud
lines: > logging in to npm as the developer...

beats.say: Pinned versions and a committed lockfile mean you only upgrade when you choose to.
Here's the prompt. Screenshot it, and send it to Claude inside your project.
Follow Ship With Pip for one of these every day.

prompt: Audit this project for npm supply chain risk. Confirm package-lock.json is committed and CI installs with npm ci. Run npm audit, list any dependency versions published in the last 7 days, and flag packages with postinstall scripts. Then propose an .npmrc with ignore-scripts=true and tell me exactly what would break.
caption: In Sept 2025 one phishing email hijacked 20 npm packages with 2B+ weekly downloads, including chalk and debug. The payload swapped crypto wallet addresses and netted about $600. A week later the Shai-Hulud worm stole tokens and cloud keys and spread itself across 500+ packages. Commit your lockfile, pin versions, rotate exposed keys, use phishing-resistant MFA. The prompt is at the end.
sources: The Hacker News, Sep 9 2025: 20 npm packages, 2B+ weekly downloads; chalk 5.6.1, debug 4.4.2, strip-ansi 7.1.1; phishing of maintainer; ~$600 stolen per Socket
